383.t: Businessmen control pop; artists were once backed
383.s: Wilson argues advertising and business-school planners now shape public taste, whereas in the thirties Hammond backed artists; he spent three hours on one solo take in 1935.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: They control the public taste through the advertising thing, and then they control the production of the product, but they can condition the buyer, too. See, it's all in the hands of the businessman now.

383.t: Where music is going and the businessmen's 'new gimmick'
383.s: Wilson reads trade-paper news of slumping fad music and predicts businessmen will take any new electronics and sell it as a gimmick, while art survives.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: gold, a million records -- that whole world has taken a dive, but the jazz is just staying on that same keel, the symphony is staying on the same keel, the classical is staying on that same keel.

383.t: Rock emphasis at Berklee and Hinton's hope for new outlets
383.s: Ted Jr. objects to rock emphasis, Wilson cites falling rock sales, and Hinton hopes theatre and dance could use jazz.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: newest issue of Variety and see if the rock movement can sell some more records, because they're firing a lot of people in the studios. In the rock recording studios, yes.

383.t: Gimmick hits: Tiny Tim and Wee Bonnie Baker
383.s: Wilson says a novelty like 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips' or 'Oh Johnny' can flare up and vanish, while real jazz endures.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: Another thing that helps to confuse what we're talking about, like we were talking about making a living, making money from this, and I was saying earlier about the rock movement going down in record sales. But you never know when gimmicks will come up, just like when Tiny Tim came up singing…

383.t: Falling pop sales, disco and the end of the fad
383.s: Wilson notes pop sales are down while jazz and classical hold steady, mocks disco strings, and predicts the pop era will run its course.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: One thing that's puzzling, I was just reading in that magazine, Billboard over there, the sales of that pop thing are down, these little record companies are firing about 1,000 people, but the jazz and classical are holding their own. They never were that big, but they don't have a big dip in jazz…

464.t: How stars were made on the bandstand versus by publicity
464.s: He contrasts stars made on the bandstand with those made by publicity machinery after the 1980s, starting with Wynton Marsalis, and says young players lead bands too soon.
464.ch: Views on the music and its business
464.q: Well I think when the overall concept of making stars changed. You see when I came up stars were made on the bandstand. You practiced your instrument at home, and you went out and played and the musicians said, “Wow, man, you hear so and-so, you know he can play his buns off, yeah.” And the…

464.t: 'Jazz in the middle ages' and neglect of mid-career musicians
464.s: He says he coined the idea of 'jazz in the middle ages', that labels sign young players while overlooking mid-career masters, and that one should keep busy with projects.
464.q: And I remember a number of years ago there was an article written in the New York Times I think it was ’88 or something, it talked about that. And at first people thought it was a joke, but they saw the seriousness of what I was speaking about and how these various musicians have been overlooked.…

741.t: Ageism and the marketing of jazz
741.s: Younger musicians are marketed like movies and shoes, which he feels cheapens the music.
741.q: I think there probably is. I think, I would almost bet that yeah. Like if I wanted to go to another label right now at my age, I might be able to land a deal with somebody, somebody might give me a shot, because I’ve got a proven track record. But an older musician trying to, who isn’t as…

1001.t: 'Young lions' hype and avoiding rock gigs
1001.s: Dislikes industry picking stars by look; never played rock, only some Top 40 at weddings.
1001.q: I don’t think so. I think it’s too bad — it’s great for them and their careers obviously. It’s too bad in a way because I feel that somebody in an office somewhere is making the decision as to who is going to be able to make it, whereas I gather that years ago it was more like the best guys were…

1007.t: Missing middle of the jazz market and the tribute-album trend
1007.s: He says booking splits between a few stars and low-paid players with little between. He complains about tribute concerts and centennials, and Davern called it necrophilia.
1007.ch: Jazz, Lincoln Center and the music market
1007.q: Coleman. There’s a handful. But there’s not. So if you don’t have giants then you’ve got people that are just being marketed very well. And if that becomes sort of your top tier, and everybody else is kind of on the bottom, there’s this huge hole in the middle. There’s $5,000 and less, and $50,000…

902.t: Novelty Latin hits, Macarena and Kenny G's Latin album
902.s: He views such hits as business moves, praising Cyndi Lauper's Latin record and doubting Kenny G's.
902.q: I see this is business you know. And he’s looking at it as the standpoint of that. Kenny G I think also, a couple of years ago recorded a Latin record, tried to do a Latin album so he could enter it into the Latin Grammys since it’s Kenny G — he thought maybe he would have a leg up on it or…

737.t: Young musicians, managers and the lost culture of standards
737.s: Record companies and managers steer young stars away from older players and standards, and his generation scattered into leaders instead of playing together.
737.ch: Church, energy and the state of jazz
737.q: guys coming out of the schools and so forth but I think that management and the music business has taken another look at it and said — hmmm, people are starting to like jazz. All those commercials I hear, everything is jazz now you know. And it’s a money making situation and most of the kids have…

497.t: How the music business has changed and lost individuality
497.s: He feels institutionalization and industry standards push musicians to look backward rather than be original.
497.q: Yes. Very much. I’m not sure it’s changed for the better. It’s changed. I have questions about it. The institutionalization of the music has been good on one end and I think it’s not good on another end. I think that the industry has standards and the concepts that they project as to what is…

502.t: Business people, American Idol and the decline of quality
502.s: He blames business graduates and promotion over craft for the music scene, noting record heads used to be musicians, and dismisses Rod Stewart's standards.
502.ch: Career, business and the music industry
502.q: Well that’s like — well I’ll tell you a bigger overview is that I think that business has conspired to bring the masses into music. They want the masses to — you know they want you to be a singer. They want everyone to be able to sing. So now instead of to get to Carnegie Hall you practice,…

350.t: Innovation, built-in obsolescence and quality: cars and Japanese goods
350.s: Murray uses the American automobile, Volkswagen, Japanese and Swiss quality to argue real innovation is quality and workmanship, and that hype sells bad music.
350.q: You see? There’s a lot of things that save us with the American automobile, once they got to a certain point. In the beginning they wanted to be durable. This will be better than a horse because the horse is going to die. So they built the automobiles that lasted as long as they could make them…

582.t: Age and marketing in jazz, and James Moody
582.s: They criticize record-label marketing of the young and neglect of older and middle-generation players, citing James Moody.
582.q: That’s a long topic to be discussed. I mean unfortunately the way things are going now in this world and with the whole marketing ploy it’s like new, exciting, these things are really being pushed through the marketing forces and things like that. And it’s very unfortunate because this art form is…

500.t: Industry hype, Jane Monheit and being 'the next Sarah'
500.s: Asked about Angela Davis's remark, she criticizes an industry that makes young singers stars overnight and insists on being her own self.
500.q: Well yes I do, and I think my reaction is more about the industry. Whether her picture was on the cover and mine wasn’t, that is not, for me not an issue. But I think the issue is that you know when I think of someone like Sarah Vaughan who was 59 years old before she won a Grammy, and she had this…

699.t: Young leaders, the apprentice period and record industry contracts
699.s: Young musicians used to apprentice with elders as Clifford Brown did; he criticizes the industry signing inexperienced youth.
699.q: we just have to be a watchdog to make sure that people understand that we cannot have this sort of cookie cutter instantaneous way of producing things.

548.t: Mainstream label and the marketing of young lions
548.s: Being labeled mainstream limits invitations; he criticizes record companies and critics for favoring some styles over others.
548.q: Right, which is fine. I mean I don’t begrudge them. I mean I think most of the ones that get the attention are extremely talented and they’re terrific players. The only thing that bothers me a little bit is that it seems like some styles count today and others don’t, and if you look at it from a…

525.t: Jazz press, youth marketing and inclusion; Kamasi Washington and Freddie Hubbard
525.s: Weiss discusses magazines and festivals favoring young acts, major labels, and Kamasi Washington's debt to Billy Harper, and says Hubbard hated being treated as a dead legend.
525.ch: The jazz business and hard bop
525.q: Cool. Absolutely. You know I mean it wasn’t this kind of conversation today but I remember within ten years I mean you know I talked to the guy at DownBeat before, the editor, Jason Koransky. And we were talking, I forgot what it was, we were joking about something but in that kind of realm you…

906.t: Joe's loyalty to jazz while others cross over
906.s: Joe never moved to rock, pop or country; she compares Harry Connick and Barry Manilow's big band album.
906.q: No, he’s never changed his belief in what he wants to do. I mean he would never go to rock ‘n roll or pop music or country & western.

552.t: The young lions era and Wynton Marsalis
552.s: Wilson on the origins of the young lions and musicians signed without apprenticeship.
552.ch: The music industry and the press
552.q: Well that point is often debated and discussed. I don’t think it was any one person. I think it was a combination of forces. Generally speaking, and I’m not going to say that Wynton Marsalis is responsible for that, he’s not. Because when Wynton came on the scene it actually was responsible for a…

135.t: Against crossover: Mtume, Grover Washington and the 'beat back in jazz'
135.s: Heath explains why he told Jimmy a crossover piece would not work, rebukes a producer's claim about dancing, and says the MJQ never compromised.
135.q: That’s Jimmy’s son, yeah, Mtume. I told Jimmy at the time, that’s why I’m anti- crossover because I feel if you have to… I was at a meeting once and Grover, rest his soul…

165.t: Jazz under attack by record company accountants
165.s: He argues commercial interests, lawyers and accountants have taken over the music business and are destroying jazz.
165.q: I think that we – jazz artists, jazz itself – we’re under attack. We’re like a city that’s being bombed, like Guernica in the Spanish Civil War, where the Germans used their new Stuka bomber just to test it out. Those people in that town didn’t know what was happening to them. They didn’t know why…

170.t: Cecil Taylor, crossover and the economics of the music
170.s: Ware and Gloria discuss crossover, Keith Jarrett, Cecil Taylor with Mary Lou Williams, and money.
170.ch: Bass playing, avant-garde and the state of the music
170.q: You know? And Keith Jarrett is coming down to that actually. It's a form of, to me, European, classical, you know? But they have never learned to call it jazz.

86.t: Erskine Hawkins, Dud Bascomb and who gets promoted
86.s: Edison says Hawkins led on his chops and promotion, not talent, and complains talent matters little in today's industry.
86.q: Yes, he is. So I think after he heard what -- well, after I went to New York, I became so engrossed in listening to the solos, going from place to place. I used to go listen to Erskine Hawkins, go listen to Charlie Shavers, go listen to Roy Eldridge.

529.t: Individuals versus group names in rock-era marketing
529.s: Ridley asks, with George Russell's view, whether group emphasis replaced individuality.
529.q: So do you--I'm not trying to lead you but I'm just trying to sort of put it into uh, a certain kind of thing of what I think I hear you say in terms of--you know, and it's still trying to tie it back to the whole thing of defining what is jazz. One of the things that you said, you mentioned about…
